stem: A nurse is caring for a stable client during early recovery after a cesarean birth. Which plan best supports detection and prevention of common postpartum and postoperative complications?

options.A: Assess the fundus, lochia, incision, bladder and bowel function, pain, and extremities, and assist with ambulation when clinically appropriate and permitted.
options.B: Focus on the incision, pain, and vital signs, and defer fundal and lochia assessment because postoperative bleeding after cesarean birth is primarily incisional.
options.C: Assess the fundus, lochia, incision, and extremities, but keep the client on bed rest during early recovery so movement does not stress the abdominal incision.
options.D: Prioritize ambulation, bowel function, and pain control, and delay routine incision assessment until drainage, fever, or increasing wound discomfort is reported.

rationale: A client recovering from cesarean birth requires routine postpartum surveillance as well as postoperative assessment. Open RN postpartum guidance includes assessment of the fundus, cesarean incision, bladder, bowel function, lochia, extremities, and pain. Postoperative guidance supports ambulation as soon as appropriate according to agency policy and provider orders and continued surveillance for venous thromboembolism and other complications. B incorrectly omits fundal and lochia assessment. C includes appropriate assessments but unnecessarily imposes bed rest, conflicting with postoperative mobility guidance. D includes helpful recovery measures but delays routine incision surveillance until symptoms appear.
educational_objective: After cesarean birth, combine routine postpartum assessment with surgical-incision and postoperative surveillance, and promote clinically appropriate early mobility rather than replacing postpartum checks or delaying wound assessment.
source_organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion [Internet], Chapter 11: Postpartum Care; Health Alterations [Internet], Chapter 2: Perioperative Care
source_locator: Nursing Health Promotion, Chapter 11 Postpartum Care > 11.5 > Focused Postpartum Assessments > Table 11.5a BUBBLE-EE: assess fundus and cesarean incision, bladder, bowels, lochia, extremities and other postpartum findings; Additional Cesarean Birth Discomforts: encourage early and frequent ambulation. Health Alterations, Chapter 2 > Table 2.5b Routine Postoperative Nursing Interventions: assist out of bed and ambulate as soon as possible according to agency policy/provider orders; provide DVT prophylaxis as prescribed and continue monitoring for signs of DVT.
source_claim_supported: Post-cesarean nursing care combines routine postpartum assessment with incision and postoperative surveillance, while clinically appropriate early ambulation and DVT monitoring support complication prevention.

supporting_sources.organization: Open Resources for Nursing (Open RN) / Chippewa Valley Technical College; hosted by NCBI Bookshelf
supporting_sources.locator: Table 2.5b Routine Postoperative Nursing Interventions: assist the client out of bed and ambulate as soon as possible according to agency policy and provider orders; administer prescribed DVT prophylaxis and continue monitoring for signs of DVT.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Early postoperative ambulation and ongoing DVT surveillance are routine measures used to reduce postoperative complication risk.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed pp. 42–45: evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; assess changes and trends in client condition; under Potential for Complications from Surgical Procedures and Health Alterations, evaluate response to postoperative interventions to prevent complications, including promoting venous return and mobility; perform focused assessments.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — postoperative/postpartum surveillance after cesarean birth
correction_summary: Rebuilt the four plans to eliminate the uniquely-long keyed answer and replace simplistic distractors with realistic errors in assessment scope, mobility, and timing of wound surveillance. The corrected item preserves integrated postpartum/postoperative monitoring after cesarean birth.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Cesarean recovery — integrated postpartum and postoperative complication surveillance
audit_findings.stem: PASS — stable early post-cesarean context and one integrated plan-of-care decision.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — includes the source-supported postpartum assessment domains and clinically appropriate mobility; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — incision and vital-sign surveillance are appropriate, but cesarean birth does not remove the need for fundal and lochia assessment.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — the assessments are appropriate, but routine bed rest conflicts with guidance to ambulate as soon as clinically appropriate.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — mobility and comfort measures are appropriate, but routine incision assessment should not wait for symptoms.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only plan that preserves both postpartum surveillance and postoperative prevention without adding a contradictory restriction or delay.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B omits core postpartum checks, C incorrectly restricts mobility, and D delays wound surveillance.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all option lengths are nearly identical and the keyed answer is not stylistically privileged.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Reduction of Risk Potential directly includes focused assessment and evaluation of postoperative interventions that promote mobility and reduce complications.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether C could be defended for immediate incision protection and whether D could be symptom-triggered; current postoperative guidance supports early mobility when appropriate and routine surveillance rather than delayed assessment, leaving A uniquely best.
